plan.title: A Note App That Works While You Think
plan.description: A launch video for a note-taking app built to cut the overhead of organizing and help you find your notes again. It shows why notes often become graveyards and how a simpler workflow fixes that.

beats.narration: Be honest. When did you last open an old note and actually use it? Most of us save and save, and then never look again.

props.title: Your notes deserve a second life
props.subtitle: Meet the note app that works while you think

beats.narration: Many people call their note apps graveyards. We take notes, but we never revisit them. Storing more feels like progress, even when nothing comes back out.

props.definition: An app where notes go in and never come out again.

beats.narration: And the work around the notes grows. Moving them, updating tags, reorganizing folders. When your system feels like a second job, the tool is demanding too much.
Then there is the split. A work app here, a personal app there, and neither has the full picture. Every search for something across both costs you a context switch.
Switching apps has always been expensive. You have to move your old notes into a new system, and it takes time. So people stay stuck with tools they have outgrown.

props.text: The cost of switching is high, so people stay stuck.

beats.narration: Notes also live next to email, Slack, and messages. Constant alt-tabbing challenges our ability to build knowledge and draw connections. A note app should calm that, not add to it.

props.alt: hands typing on a laptop with many windows

beats.narration: So we built our app around three simple ideas. Capture fast. Find anything instantly. And bring your notes back to you at the moment you need them.
First, capture. Open the app, type or paste, and you are done. No folders to pick, no tags to remember. You write the thought and move on.
Second, retrieval. Ask for what you remember, in your own words. AI retrieval makes reviewing effortless, so notes that go in finally come back out.

turns.speaker: You
turns.text: What did I note about the launch plan?

turns.speaker: App
turns.text: Here are your notes on it, from work and home.

beats.narration: Third, one home for everything. Work and personal notes sit together, so the full picture is always there. No more paying the context switching tax.
And leaving your old app is painless. Many note apps let you export your notes as Markdown, so moving your notes over does not mean starting from zero.
One honest point. No app fixes a missing habit. If you are not capturing anything, a new tool is just a different empty app. The habit still starts with you.

props.text: No app fixes the note-taking habit.

beats.narration: What we can do is remove the friction. Less time organizing, more time thinking. A tool that stays out of your way, so the habit is easier to keep.

props.heading: Less friction, better habit
items: A tool out of your way

beats.narration: So here is the idea. Stop filing notes into a graveyard. Capture quickly, find anything, and let your notes come back to you. Try the app today, and write your first note.

hook_close.hook_text: Be honest. When did you last open an old note and actually use it? Most of us save and save, and then never look again.
hook_close.close_text: So here is the idea. Stop filing notes into a graveyard. Capture quickly, find anything, and let your notes come back to you. Try the app today, and write your first note.

accuracy.reason: The script presents product features (AI retrieval, one search across work and personal notes, no folders) as the user's own app, which the brief never specified. It also attributes a generic Mem quote to the app's pitch, and the Markdown export claim is hedged only with 'many'.

coverage.reason: It has a problem, solution, benefit arc and a CTA, but there is no app name, no placeholder flags, no pricing or platform info, and no concrete demo. The problem section runs long (beats 1-6) relative to the product section.

structure.reason: Chapters run problem, why switching felt hard, what changes, honest note and start today. The flow is clear, though beat 2 and beat 3 overlap somewhat and beat 12 slows momentum before the CTA.

hook_ending.reason: The opener 'When did you last open an old note and actually use it?' is a good tension-creating question. The ending's 'graveyard' callback with a CTA works, though 'write your first note' is somewhat soft.

tone.reason: Conversational and brand-appropriate for a launch video, with a candid 'honest note' beat. The tone is slightly generic marketing.

visuals.reason: Scene types vary well. However, the versus table with 'No/No', 'Slow/Slow' and 'Constant/Constant' rows is a weak comparison, the diagram edge labels 'stored' and 'retrieved' do not match the nodes, and the clip query is generic.

originality.reason: The 'note graveyard' and 'second job' framing is lifted from the sources. The content is mostly competitor-blog language repurposed, with no unique product detail.

instructions.reason: It is a launch video of roughly the right length, but it invents product capabilities without flagging them as placeholders and never names the app.

language.reason: Clean, natural English with short punchy sentences. There are minor fragment-heavy rhythms.

defects.quote: AI retrieval makes reviewing effortless, so notes that go in finally come back out.
defects.issue: This is a claim lifted from Mem's marketing and presented as the new app's feature, with no basis in the brief.
A competitor's line is attributed on screen inside the launch video for a different app, which is confusing and wrongly implies endorsement.

defects.quote: So we built our app around three simple ideas.
defects.issue: The script invents specific product features without flagging them as placeholders and never names the app.
The versus table has identical values on both sides, so it shows no contrast.
The edge labels do not match the 'capture, find, resurface' flow described in the narration.

defects.quote: Try the app today, and write your first note.
defects.issue: The call to action gives no concrete next step such as a platform, download or price.

defects.quote: Many people call their note apps graveyards.
defects.issue: This repeats the beat 1 point that people never revisit their notes, and the problem section drags.

missing: A concrete use-case story or demo
Pricing or a clear call-to-action link
wrong_facts: Mem's quote is attributed within another app's launch video; the features (AI retrieval, one search) are unverified for the unnamed app.
judge.summary: A well-structured problem-solution arc with a good hook, but it borrows Mem's marketing claims and quote and invents features without flagging them as placeholders. Visuals are mostly sensible but a few are weak.
